aboutH2: ‘Namgis Wellness Centre: First Nations Addiction Treatment in Alert Bay
intro: The villages of the ‘Namgis were organized into extended family units (‘na’mima) each sharing a single Big House. The ceremonies and rituals of the Potlatch regulated all aspects of ‘Namgis social life. Central to that social life was a reverence for the natural world. For example, when taking and using anything of the natural world the ‘Namgis always thanked the spirits inhabiting those things for giving themselves up for use by the ‘Namgis. The first European settlement and the establishment of a non-aboriginal economy amidst the ‘Namgis began in the 1880s. The first industry to be established was a fish saltry at Alert Bay on Cormorant Island. Since that time the ‘Namgis have been intimately involved in virtually every part of the economic life of the North Island. It was as a result of their involvement in the local economy and as well as the influence of missionaries, that the ‘Namgis people have since abandoned their village at Xwalk at the mouth of the Nimpkish River. The ‘Namgis now reside at their village called ‘Yalis at Alert Bay. The traditional territory of the ‘Namgis and the resources contained therein continue to be a vital part of their culture and social life today.

pillars.title: A New Wellness Centre in ‘Yalis
pillars.body: Most ‘Namgis members live in ‘Yalis, the ‘Namgis name for Cormorant Island and the village of Alert Bay. The Nation is replacing its old treatment centre with a purpose-built Wellness Centre, planned after asking staff and community members what they needed, and the answer was more room, including space for ceremony and traditional healing. The FNHA describes two buildings joined by a common courtyard: a residential building with 16 beds and a night attendant, and a main building with reception, counselling and gathering rooms and a commercial kitchen. Construction began in May 2024. As of October 2026 the Nation had not announced that the new building is open, so ask intake where the program is running.

pillars.title: Planning for Life at Home
pillars.body: Aftercare planning and case management are part of the program, and one of its themes is self-help after treatment, including Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous and Adult Children of Alcoholics. For people who live on Cormorant Island, the Nation's Mental Health Department offers counselling at no cost for grief, trauma, depression, anxiety and drug or alcohol addiction. The Nation also lists Ne’nagwa̱’nakwa̱la (Going Home) as support for people coming home from treatment or corrections.

pillars.title: A Team That Works Layer by Layer
pillars.body: Wellness Centre staff write that alcohol and drug use is often a symptom, with trauma, neglect and abuse underneath it, and that healing has to happen layer by layer, with patience. In 2026 the team took two days of training on preventing bullying and harassment and on lateral violence and lateral kindness, led by a former FNHA occupational health and safety program leader. Applications and questions go to the intake coordinator, Em Crowell.

overview: The ‘Namgis Wellness Centre is the residential addiction treatment program of ‘Namgis First Nation (spelled ‘Na̱mg̱is by the Nation). Until 2025 it was the ‘Namgis Treatment Centre, and this site listed it as Namgis First Nation, Substance Abuse Treatment Centre. Its mission, rooted in ‘Namgis culture and traditions and with respect for individual choices and responsibilities, is to support the emotional, mental, physical and spiritual well-being of the people it serves. It is one of the FNHA-funded First Nations treatment centres in BC and runs a six-week residential program.
serviceCaption: 12 services · from the FNHA and Pathways BC listings
afterOverview: Staff explain the new name this way. The old name came from the medical model of recovery, which centres on abstinence and fits with Twelve Step programs, and abstinence is still a core goal. Over the years, though, they came to see alcohol and drug use as a way of coping with deeper pain, much of it from intergenerational trauma, Residential Schools and the Sixties Scoop. The six-week program works through themes that include the physiological and psychological effects of mood-altering substances, family dynamics, historical influences on substance abuse, spirituality, self-awareness in the cycle of change, and trauma and its long-term and short-term effects.

location.heading: ‘Namgis Wellness Centre in Alert Bay, British Columbia
location.intro: The ‘Namgis Wellness Centre is in Alert Bay on Cormorant Island, off the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, and the last leg is a BC Ferries crossing of about 45 minutes from Port McNeill. From Vancouver, plan on 8 to 9 hours with the Horseshoe Bay to Nanaimo ferry, about 4 hours of driving up Highway 19 and the Alert Bay ferry; Port Hardy is about 40 minutes from the Port McNeill terminal and Campbell River about 2 hours.

faqIntro: Answers come from the Nation's own website and public listings. Still unsure? Call, it's free and confidential.

faqs.q: Is the ‘Namgis Wellness Centre the same as the ‘Namgis Treatment Centre?
faqs.a: Yes. The Nation renamed its treatment centre the ‘Namgis Wellness Centre in 2025 as a new building neared completion, and the application form is still called the Treatment Centre Adult Referral Application Package. The FNHA's list of First Nations treatment centres still uses the old name.

faqs.q: Who can attend the ‘Namgis Wellness Centre?
faqs.a: The program is for adults 19 and older with substance use issues who apply through a referral worker. The Pathways BC listing for North Vancouver Island says the program is fully funded for clients with a Status card and does not accept Non-Status clients at this time. The FNHA referral package lists men-only and women-only sessions, so ask the intake coordinator which session fits you.

No fee is published. The centre is one of the FNHA-funded First Nations treatment centres in BC, and Pathways BC lists it as no cost for clients with a Status card. Your referral worker arranges travel to the program, including return travel if you leave early.
The residential program runs for six weeks. The new residential building has 16 beds, according to the FNHA.

faqs.q: Does the ‘Namgis Wellness Centre offer detox?
faqs.a: No. You need to be clear of medical detox before you arrive. The FNHA referral package (June 2025) asks for 14 days substance-free, while the older Pathways BC listing says 10 days, so confirm the current rule with intake.

faqs.q: Can I attend if I take methadone or Suboxone?
faqs.a: Probably not. The FNHA referral package lists the ‘Namgis program as not offering opioid agonist treatment (OAT), and Pathways BC says prescribed narcotics are not dispensed during the program. If you are on OAT, ask your referral worker about FNHA-funded centres that accept it.

Download the Treatment Centre Adult Referral Application Package from the Nation's Health & Wellness page and complete it with your referral worker. Pathways BC notes that self-referrals are not accepted, that a full physical exam is required, and that people living in the area without a referral worker can call the intake coordinator to get started. Questions go to Em Crowell at nwcintake@namgis.bc.ca or 778-401-1120.

faqs.q: Where is the centre and how do I get there?
faqs.a: The centre is in Alert Bay on Cormorant Island, which you reach by a BC Ferries crossing of about 45 minutes from Port McNeill. From Vancouver, allow 8 to 9 hours including the Horseshoe Bay to Nanaimo ferry and the drive up Highway 19, and from Port Hardy about 40 minutes to the Port McNeill terminal.

faqs.q: What happens after the program ends?
faqs.a: Aftercare planning is part of the program, and its themes include self-help groups such as AA, NA and Adult Children of Alcoholics. Alert Bay residents can also see the Nation's Mental Health Department for free counselling, and Ne’nagwa̱’nakwa̱la (Going Home) supports people returning home from treatment or corrections.

Staff say the old name came from the medical model, which focuses on abstinence, and abstinence is still a core goal. They now see substance use as often a symptom of trauma, neglect and abuse, so the work is about healing that pain layer by layer, and wellness is what they hope replaces the need for substances.

faqs.q: How do I contact the ‘Namgis Wellness Centre?
faqs.a: Call the intake coordinator at 778-401-1120, Monday to Friday from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, or 778-912-6510 after hours and on weekends. You can email nwcintake@namgis.bc.ca or fax 250-974-2257. The ‘Namgis Health Centre front desk at 250-974-5522 can also point you to the right team.
